papers.title: Rotor-driven piecewise cross polarization of wide quadrupolar lines: bath-contact pumping of vector and tensor order in dynamically polarized solids
papers.abstract: In a dynamically polarized solid with a common nuclear spin temperature, spin-1 $^{14}$N in ammonia sits at $P_N\simeq0.14$ when the protons are at $0.90$, and a deuteron in a proton-rich matrix at $P_D\simeq0.29$. Hartmann--Hahn cross polarization (CP) from the protons could raise either toward $P_H$, but the first-order quadrupole interaction spreads the $^{14}$N line over $5$~MHz at $5$~T, far beyond any single contact bandwidth. We develop the theory of CP into one transition of a quadrupolar spin-1, with slow sample rotation carrying each crystallite through a fixed-frequency contact window. A bath contact is an idempotent map on the populations of the contacted transition, so repeated or continuous contacts accumulate rather than cancel, and the hit-once and parity constraints that force stepped rotation for pulsed inversions do not arise. In the small-reservoir limit the population ratio across the contacted transition becomes $(1+P_H)/(1-P_H)$, giving $\Pzz=+0.88$ in one contact and $\Pzz\to-1.8$ in two from $P_H=0.9$, beyond the unitary bound $[-0.85,+0.65]$. Under continuous rotation, a window at the Pake horn reaches every bond for an axis perpendicular to the field, while a window in the clean pedestal region, needed for a definite sign of tensor order, reaches a fraction $\sin2\theta_c=0.943$ at the magic angle $54.74\degree$. Steady-state order is set by the contact rate against rotation-driven cross-branch relaxation, negligible for $^{14}$N. In the cubic limit one contact places the spin-1 at the proton temperature ($\Pzz=+0.85$), but only a resolved quadrupole splitting permits negative tensor order. The limiting resource is the proton spin lock, which must far exceed the $\simeq28$~kHz local field for a contact short compared with $T_{1\rho}$, unmeasured at $1$~K. Protocols are given for $^{14}$N in NH$_3$ and deuterons in NH$_2$D.

papers.title: Optical trapping of neutral atoms via magnetic-dipole transitions
papers.abstract: Optical trapping of neutral atoms is almost universally described as an electric-dipole (E1) effect. We show that the magnetic field of light, acting on a magnetic-dipole (M1) transition, can induce an ac Zeeman shift significantly larger than the ac Stark shift, thereby enabling magnetic trapping. We construct the M1 polarizability tensor and identify a critical detuning $\delta_c$, independent of optical power, below which the magnetic interaction dominates. We analyze suitable trapping parameters and possible loss mechanisms, particularly for the intraconfigurational transitions $^3H_6\rightarrow{}^3H_5$ of erbium at $1437.13$~nm and $^5I_8\rightarrow{}^5I_7$ of dysprosium at $2418.84$~nm. We propose two trapping configurations: a hybrid magnetic/electric optical tweezer and an optical lattice with separated magnetic and electric antinodes, producing state-dependent purely magnetic and purely electric trapping wells. Our results present optical magnetic fields as a suitable resource to expand the toolbox for atomic manipulation.

papers.title: Quantum-logic detection of rotationally inelastic collisions of single molecules
papers.abstract: Collisions between molecules govern chemical reactions and energy transfer across a range of different environments from interstellar space to the Earth's atmosphere. Despite their fundamental importance, molecular collisions have traditionally been studied through ensemble-averaged experiments which obscure the dynamics of individual scattering events on the quantum level. Probing single molecular collisions with quantum-state resolution has thus far remained a major experimental challenge. Here, we demonstrate a method for detecting individual rotationally inelastic collisions of single molecular ions with neutral atoms using quantum-logic techniques. We prepare individual trapped N$_2^+$ ions in their rotational ground state, subject them to a beam of helium atoms and detect isolated collision events through their effects on the motion of the trapped ions. Quantum-logic-spectroscopic measurements reveal changes of the molecular state upon collision enabling the determination of the probability of rotationally inelastic scattering. The experiments are analysed by comparison with quantum and classical scattering calculations yielding detailed insights into the underlying collision dynamics. By combining single-collision detection with non-destructive readout of the molecular quantum state, our approach establishes a new experimental framework for investigating molecular scattering beyond conventional ensemble measurements. It opens a route towards investigating state-to-state scattering in individual molecules and exploring molecular interactions at the level of single quantum-state resolved events.

papers.title: Buffer-Gas-Assisted Fluorescence Spectroscopy of Molecular Ions
papers.abstract: Sustained fluorescence detection of generic molecules has been challenging due to the lack of cycling transitions and limited photon budgets. We demonstrate a nondestructive method for continuous fluorescence of strongly rovibronically open molecular ions, $^{232}$ThF$^+$. Effective quasi-cycling transitions are established by room-temperature buffer-gas collisions, which replenish the population back to the laser-addressed states. In situ images and rotationally resolved spectra are obtained without optical repumping or auxiliary atomic readout ions. Combined with low-background spectroscopic detection, this approach achieves a signal-to-noise ratio of approximately 6 in a 1 s exposure on the P(1) line of $^{232}$ThF$^+$, despite a thermal population of only approximately 0.17% in the addressed state at room temperature. The ability to repeatedly interrogate trapped ions is particularly promising for scarce molecular samples, broadband spectroscopic searches, and in situ monitoring of molecular reactions.

papers.title: Laser cooling of $\mathrm{Th}^{-}$: Revised bound-state structure and a more efficient cooling scheme
papers.abstract: The thorium anion ($\mathrm{Th}^{-}$) has been proposed as a candidate for laser cooling of negative ions. However, previous theoretical and experimental results exhibit significant discrepancies in both the excitation energies and lifetimes. Here we revisit the bound-state structure and transition properties of $\mathrm{Th}^{-}$ using two independent ab initio approaches. The two calculations agree well and improve agreement with measured excitation energies and lifetimes. Based on the present level structure, we reassign several observed levels and show that the previously proposed $^4F^e_{3/2}\leftrightarrow{}^2S^o_{1/2}$ cooling transition is not closed and requires two repumping lasers. We therefore propose an alternative cooling scheme based on the $^4F^e_{3/2}\leftrightarrow{}^4F^o_{3/2}$ transition, which requires only one repumping laser and has a transition rate approximately five times larger ($A\approx1.1\times10^5$ s$^{-1}$), the fastest reported bound--bound E1 transition in atomic anions to date.

papers.title: Spectroscopy of ultracold molecules in the mid-infrared
papers.abstract: Unlike the microwave and optical domains, frequency metrology in the mid-infrared has not yet benefited from the long coherence times and exquisite control provided by ultracold particles. We use a quantum cascade laser operating at 17.5 THz to drive ro-vibrational transitions in ultracold calcium monofluoride molecules. The laser linewidth is narrowed to 15 kHz by locking it to a custom mid-infrared ring cavity, which is in turn locked to an ultrastable laser. We study the spectrum for molecules confined in red-detuned and blue-detuned magneto-optical traps, and in an optical dipole trap. In the dipole trap, the spectroscopic linewidth is close to that of the laser. We consider the stability and accuracy that can be reached using these methods in the context of a broader programme for improving frequency metrology in the mid-infrared.

papers.title: Critical excited states in quantum metrology
papers.abstract: We investigate criticality-enhanced sensing near ground- and excited-state quantum phase transitions in a strongly coupled qubit-boson system. Accounting for finite-size effects, we design driving protocols that exploit diverging susceptibilities to enhance signal-to-noise ratios in parameter estimation using experimentally relevant generators. We show that the excited-state criticality provides a metrological advantage through single-mode bosonic squeezing in regimes that circumvent the 'death of adiabaticity', limiting conventional critical quantum metrology with ground-state criticality.

papers.title: Dual-species atom interferometry for axion dark matter
papers.abstract: Atom interferometers are sensitive to oscillations of the masses and transition frequencies of atoms, which can be induced by axion dark matter. The main limitation is the sensitivity to gravity gradient noise (GGN). We propose a dual-species atom interferometry sequence that provides a suppression of GGN by up to three orders of magnitude and a sensitivity enhancement via the mass difference of the two atoms. We show that, under realistic experimental assumptions, a 10m-baseline dual-species atom interferometer is more sensitive to the axion gluon coupling than a 100m single-species gradiometer. Including a comprehensive noise analysis, we demonstrate that the Very Long Baseline Atom Interferometer (VLBAI) in Hannover with a baseline of 10m can probe the axion decay constant at levels almost competitive with leading laboratory constraints. The proposed 100m-baseline Atom Interferometer CERN Experiment (AICE) can extend this sensitivity by up to two orders of magnitude, surpassing laboratory constraints for axion masses of $10^{-19}\;\text{eV}/c^2 \lesssim m_a \lesssim 3\times10^{-15}\;\text{eV}/c^2$.
